markdown.markdown: ```{r, echo = T, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE} library(ISLR) library(tidymodels) library(DALEXtra) co <- read.table("data/co.dat", col.names = c("age", "pop"), header = FALSE) ``` ## Non-linear relationships ::: question What have we used so far to deal with non-linear relationships? ::: . . . Polynomials! ## Polynomials {.smaller} $$y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_i + \beta_2x_i^2+\beta_3x_i^3 \dots + \beta_dx_i^d+\epsilon_i$$ . . . :::{.panel-tabset} ### Plot ```{r, echo = FALSE,out.width= "70%"} #| fig-height: 4.5 ggplot(co, aes(age, pop)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(formula = y ~ poly(x, 4), method = "lm") ``` ### Code ```{r, eval = F} ggplot(co, aes(age, pop)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(formula = y ~ poly(x, 4), method = "lm") ``` :::{.aside} This is data from the Columbia World Fertility Survey (1975-76) to examine household compositions ::: ::: ## How is it done? {.small} - New variables are created ( $X_1 = X$, $X_2 = X^2$, $X_3 = X^3$, etc) and treated as multiple linear regression - We are *not* interested in the individual coefficients, we are interested in how a *specific* $x$ value behaves - $\hat{f}(x_0) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1x_0 + \hat\beta_2x_0^2 + \hat\beta_3x_0^3 + \hat\beta_4x_0^4$ - *or more often a change between two values*, $a$ and $b$ - $\hat{f}(b) -\hat{f}(a) = \hat\beta_1b + \hat\beta_2b^2 + \hat\beta_3b^3 + \hat\beta_4b^4 - \hat\beta_1a - \hat\beta_2a^2 - \hat\beta_3a^3 -\hat\beta_4a^4$ - $\hat{f}(b) -\hat{f}(a) =\hat\beta_1(b-a) + \hat\beta_2(b^2-a^2)+\hat\beta_3(b^3-a^3)+\hat\beta_4(b^4-a^4)$ ## Polynomial Regression {.small} $$\hat{f}(b) -\hat{f}(a) =\hat\beta_1(b-a) + \hat\beta_2(b^2-a^2)+\hat\beta_3(b^3-a^3)+\hat\beta_4(b^4-a^4)$$ ::: question How do you pick $a$ and $b$? ::: - If given no other information, a sensible choice may be the 25th and 75th percentiles of $x$ ## Polynomial Regression :::{.panel-tabset} ### Plot ```{r, echo = FALSE} ggplot(co, aes(x = age, y = pop)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(formula = y ~ poly(x, 4), method = "lm") + geom_vline(xintercept = c(24.5, 73.5), lty = 2) ``` ### Code ```{r, eval = FALSE} ggplot(co, aes(x = age, y = pop)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(formula = y ~ poly(x, 4), method = "lm") + geom_vline(xintercept = c(24.5, 73.5), lty = 2) ``` ::: ## `Application Exercise` {.smaller} $$pop = \beta_0 + \beta_1age + \beta_2age^2 + \beta_3age^3 +\beta_4age^4+ \epsilon$$ . . . ::: question Using the information below, write out the equation to predicted change in population from a change in age from the 25th percentile (24.5) to a 75th percentile (73.5). ::: :::{.panel-tabset} ### Model Result ```{r, echo = FALSE} lm(pop ~ age + I(age^2) + I(age^3) + I(age^4), data = co) %>% tidy() %>% knitr::kable(digits = 4, format = "markdown") ``` ### Code ```{r, eval = FALSE} lm(pop ~ age + I(age^2) + I(age^3) + I(age^4), data = co) %>% tidy() ``` ::: ## Choosing $d$ {.small} $$y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_i + \beta_2x_i^2+\beta_3x_i^3 \dots + \beta_dx_i^d+\epsilon_i$$ ### Either: ::: nonincremental - Pre-specify $d$ (before looking `r emo::ji("eyes")` at your data!) - Use cross-validation to pick $d$ (take statistical learning!) ::: . . . ::: question Why before looking? ::: ## Polynomial Regression Polynomials have notoriously bad tail behavior (so they can be bad for extrapolation) . . . ::: question What does this mean? ::: ## Step functions {.smaller} Another way to create a transformation is to cut the variable into distinct regions $$C_1(X) = I(X < 35), C_2(X) = I(35\leq X<65), C_3(X) = I(X \geq 65)$$ . . . :::{.panel-tabset} ### Plot ```{r, echo = FALSE,out.width="60%"} #| fig-height: 4.5 mod <- lm(pop ~ I(age < 35) + I(age >=35 & age < 65) + I(age >= 65), data = co) p <- predict(mod) ggplot(co, aes(x = age, y = pop)) + geom_point() + geom_line(aes(x = age, y = p), color = "blue") ``` ### Code ```{r, eval = FALSE} mod <- lm(pop ~ I(age < 35) + I(age >=35 & age < 65) + I(age >= 65), data = co) p <- predict(mod) ggplot(co, aes(x = age, y = pop)) + geom_point() + geom_line(aes(x = age, y = p), color = "blue") ``` ::: ## Step functions {.small} - Create dummy variables for each group - Include each of these variables in multiple regression - The choice of cutpoints or **knots** can be problematic (and make a big difference!) ## Step functions {.small} $$C_1(X) = I(X < 35), C_2(X) = I(35\leq X<65), C_3(X) = I(X \geq 65)$$ :::{.panel-tabset} ### Plot ```{r, echo = FALSE} #| fig-height: 2.5 mod <- lm(pop ~ I(age < 35) + I(age >=35 & age < 65) + I(age >= 65), data = co) p <- predict(mod) ggplot(co, aes(x = age, y = pop)) + geom_point() + geom_line(aes(x = age, y = p), color = "blue") ``` ### Code ```{r, eval = FALSE} mod <- lm(pop ~ I(age < 35) + I(age >=35 & age < 65) + I(age >= 65), data = co) p <- predict(mod) ggplot(co, aes(x = age, y = pop)) + geom_point() + geom_line(aes(x = age, y = p), color = "blue") ``` ::: . . . ::: question What is the predicted value when $age = 25$? ::: ## Step functions {.small} $$C_1(X) = I(X < 15), C_2(X) = I(15\leq X<65), C_3(X) = I(X \geq 65)$$ :::{.panel-tabset} ### Plot ```{r, echo = FALSE} #| fig-height: 2.5 mod <- lm(pop ~ I(age < 15) + I(age >=15 & age < 65) + I(age >= 65), data = co) p <- predict(mod) ggplot(co, aes(x = age, y = pop)) + geom_point() + geom_line(aes(x = age, y = p), color = "blue") ``` ### Code ```{r, eval = FALSE} mod <- lm(pop ~ I(age < 15) + I(age >=15 & age < 65) + I(age >= 65), data = co) p <- predict(mod) ggplot(co, aes(x = age, y = pop)) + geom_point() + geom_line(aes(x = age, y = p), color = "blue") ``` ::: . . . ::: question What is the predicted value when $age = 25$? ::: ## Piecewise polynomials {.small} Instead of a single polynomial in $X$ over it's whole domain, we can use different polynomials in regions defined by knots $$y_i = \begin{cases}\beta_{01}+\beta_{11}x_i + \beta_{21}x^2_i+\beta_{31}x^3_i+\epsilon_i& \textrm{if } x_i < c\\ \beta_{02}+\beta_{12}x_i + \beta_{22}x_i^2 + \beta_{32}x_{i}^3+\epsilon_i&\textrm{if }x_i\geq c\end{cases}$$ ::: question What could go wrong here? ::: - It would be nice to have constraints (like continuity!) - Insert **splines!** ## Examples ![](img/splines.png) ## Linear Splines {.small} *A linear spline with knots at* $\xi_k$, $k = 1,\dots, K$ is a piecewise linear polynomial continuous at each knot $$y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1b_1(x_i)+\beta_2b_2(x_i)+\dots+\beta_{K+1}b_{K+1}(x_i)+\epsilon_i$$ - $b_k$ are **basis functions** - $\begin{align}b_1(x_i)&=x_i\\ b_{k+1}(x_i)&=(x_i-\xi_k)_+,k=1,\dots,K\end{align}$ - Here $()_+$ means the **positive part** - $(x_i-\xi_k)_+=\begin{cases}x_i-\xi_k & \textrm{if } x_i>\xi_k\\0&\textrm{otherwise}\end{cases}$ ## `Application Exercise` {.small} Let's create data set to fit a *linear spline* with 2 knots: 35 and 65. :::: columns ::: {.column width="20%"} | x | |-----| | 4 | | 15 | | 25 | | 37 | | 49 | | 66 | |70 | |80 | ::: ::: {.column width="80%"} ::: nonincremental 1. Using the data to the left create a new dataset with three variables: $b_1(x), b_2(x), b_3(x)$ 2. Write out the equation you would be fitting to estimate the effect on some outcome $y$ using this linear spline ::: ::: :::: ## Linear Spline :::: columns ::: {.column width="20%"} | x | |-----| | 4 | | 15 | | 25 | | 37 | | 49 | | 66 | |70 | |80 | ::: ::: {.column width="10%"} ### `r emo::ji("right_arrow")` ::: ::: {.column width="70%"} | $b_1(x)$| $b_2(x)$ | $b_3(x)$| |-----|--------------|---------| | 4 | 0 | 0 | 15 | 0 | 0 | 25 | 0 | 0 | 37 | 2 | 0 | 49 | 14 | 0 | 66 | 31 | 1 |70 | 35 | 5 |80 | 45 | 15 ::: :::: ## `Application Exercise` {.small} Below is a linear regression model fit to include the 3 bases you just created with 2 knots: 35 and 65. Use the information here to draw the relationship between $x$ and $y$. :::{.panel-tabset} ### Result ```{r} #| echo: false set.seed(1) d <- tibble( b1 = c(4, 15, 25, 37, 49, 66, 70, 80), b2 = ifelse(b1 < 35, 0, b1 - 35), b3 = ifelse(b1 < 65, 0, b1 - 65), y = 2 * b1 + -2 * b2 -3 * b3 + rnorm(8, sd = 0.25) ) lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3, data = d) |> tidy() |> knitr::kable(digits = 1) ``` ### Code ```{r} #| eval: false set.seed(1) d <- tibble( b1 = c(4, 15, 25, 37, 49, 66, 70, 80), b2 = ifelse(b1 < 35, 0, b1 - 35), b3 = ifelse(b1 < 65, 0, b1 - 65), y = 2 * b1 + -2 * b2 -3 * b3 + rnorm(8, sd = 0.25) ) lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3, data = d) |> tidy() |> knitr::kable(digits = 1) ``` ::: ## Linear Splines {.small} ::: {.column width="70%"} | $b_1(x)$| $b_2(x)$ | $b_3(x)$| $\hat{y}$ |-----|--------------|---------| | 4 | 0 | 0 | $2 \times 4 -2 \times 0 - 3\times 0 = 8$ | 15 | 0 | 0 | $2 \times 15 -2 \times 0 - 3\times 0 = 30$ | 25 | 0 | 0 | $2 \times 25 -2 \times 0 - 3\times 0 = 50$ | 37 | 2 | 0 | $2 \times 37 -2 \times 2 - 3\times 0 = 70$ | 49 | 14 | 0 | $2 \times 49 -2 \times 14 - 3\times 0 = 70$ | 66 | 31 | 1 | $2 \times 66 -2 \times 31 - 3\times 1 = 67$ |70 | 35 | 5 | $2 \times 70 -2 \times 35 - 3\times 5 = 55$ |80 | 45 | 15 | $2 \times 80 -2 \times 45 - 3\times 15 = 25$ ::: ## Linear Splines {.small} :::{.panel-tabset} ### Plot ```{r} #| echo: false p_ <- predict(lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3, data = d)) ggplot(d, aes(x = b1, y = p_)) + geom_point() + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y))) ``` ### Code ```{r} #| eval: false p_ <- predict(lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3, data = d)) ggplot(d, aes(x = b1, y = p_)) + geom_point() + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y))) ``` ::: ## Linear Splines {.small} :::{.panel-tabset} ### Plot ```{r} #| echo: false newdat <- tibble( b1 = 4:80, b2 = ifelse(b1 > 35, b1 - 35, 0), b3 = ifelse(b1 > 65, b1 - 65, 0) ) p <- predict(lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3, data = d), newdata = newdat) ggplot(newdat, aes(x = b1, y = p)) + geom_point() + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y))) ``` ### Code ```{r} #| eval: false newdat <- tibble( b1 = 4:80, b2 = ifelse(b1 > 35, b1 - 35, 0), b3 = ifelse(b1 > 65, b1 - 65, 0) ) p <- predict(lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3, data = d), newdata = newdat) ggplot(newdat, aes(x = b1, y = p)) + geom_point() + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y))) ``` ::: ## Cubic Splines {.small} *A cubic splines with knots at* $\xi_i, k = 1, \dots, K$ is a piecewise cubic polynomial with continuous derivatives up to order 2 at each knot. Again we can represent this model with truncated power functions $$y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1b_1(x_i)+\beta_2b_2(x_i)+\dots+\beta_{K+3}b_{K+3}(x_i) + \epsilon_i$$ $$\begin{align}b_1(x_i)&=x_i\\b_2(x_i)&=x_i^2\\b_3(x_i)&=x_i^3\\b_{k+3}(x_i)&=(x_i-\xi_k)^3_+, k = 1,\dots,K\end{align}$$ where $$(x_i-\xi_k)^{3}_+=\begin{cases}(x_i-\xi_k)^3&\textrm{if }x_i>\xi_k\\0&\textrm{otherwise}\end{cases}$$ ## `Application Exercise` {.small} Let's create data set to fit a *cubic spline* with 2 knots: 35 and 65. :::: columns ::: {.column width="20%"} | x | |-----| | 4 | | 15 | | 25 | | 37 | | 49 | | 66 | |70 | |80 | ::: ::: {.column width="80%"} ::: nonincremental 1. Using the data to the left create a new dataset with five variables: $b_1(x), b_2(x), b_3(x), b_4(x), b_5(x)$ 2. Write out the equation you would be fitting to estimate the effect on some outcome *y* using this cubic spline ::: ::: :::: ## Cubic Spline {.smaller} :::{.panel-tabset} ### Example :::: columns ::: {.column width="20%"} | x | |-----| | 4 | | 15 | | 25 | | 37 | | 49 | | 66 | |70 | |80 | ::: ::: {.column width="10%"} #### `r emo::ji("right_arrow")` ::: ::: {.column width="70%"} ```{r} #| echo: false d |> mutate(b2 = b1^2, b3 = b1^3, b4 = ifelse(b1 > 35, (b1 - 35)^3, 0), b5 = ifelse(b1 > 65, (b1 - 65)^3, 0) ) -> d d |> select(-y) |> knitr::kable() ``` ::: :::: ### Code ```{r} #| eval: false d |> mutate(b2 = b1^2, b3 = b1^3, b4 = ifelse(b1 > 35, (b1 - 35)^3, 0), b5 = ifelse(b1 > 65, (b1 - 65)^3, 0) ) -> d d |> select(-y) |> knitr::kable() ``` ::: ## Cubic Spline {.small} :::{.panel-tabset} ### Fit Result ```{r} #| echo: false lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3 + b4 + b5, data = d) |> tidy() |> knitr::kable(digits = 3) ``` ### Code ```{r} #| eval: false lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3 + b4 + b5, data = d) |> tidy() |> knitr::kable(digits = 3) ``` ::: ## Cubic Splines {.small} :::{.panel-tabset} ### Plot ```{r} #| echo: false p_ <- predict(lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3 + b4 + b5, data = d)) ggplot(d, aes(x = b1, y = p_)) + geom_point() + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y))) ``` ### Code ```{r} #| eval: false p_ <- predict(lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3 + b4 + b5, data = d)) ggplot(d, aes(x = b1, y = p_)) + geom_point() + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y))) ``` ::: ## Cubic Splines {.small} :::{.panel-tabset} ### Plot ```{r} #| echo: false newdat <- tibble( b1 = 4:80, b2 = b1^2, b3 = b1^3, b4 = ifelse(b1 > 35, (b1 - 35)^3, 0), b5 = ifelse(b1 > 65, (b1 - 65)^3, 0) ) p <- predict(lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3 + b4 + b5, data = d), newdata = newdat) ggplot(newdat, aes(x = b1, y = p)) + geom_point() + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y))) ``` ### Code ```{r} #| eval: false newdat <- tibble( b1 = 4:80, b2 = b1^2, b3 = b1^3, b4 = ifelse(b1 > 35, (b1 - 35)^3, 0), b5 = ifelse(b1 > 65, (b1 - 65)^3, 0) ) p <- predict(lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3 + b4 + b5, data = d), newdata = newdat) ggplot(newdat, aes(x = b1, y = p)) + geom_point() + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y))) ``` ::: ## Cubic Splines {.small} :::{.panel-tabset} ### Plot ```{r} #| echo: false newdat <- tibble( b1 = -100:100, b2 = b1^2, b3 = b1^3, b4 = ifelse(b1 > 35, (b1 - 35)^3, 0), b5 = ifelse(b1 > 65, (b1 - 65)^3, 0) ) p <- predict(lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3 + b4 + b5, data = d), newdata = newdat) ggplot(newdat, aes(x = b1, y = p)) + geom_point() + geom_vline(xintercept = c(4, 80), lty = 2) + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y))) ``` ### Code ```{r} #| eval: false newdat <- tibble( b1 = -100:100, b2 = b1^2, b3 = b1^3, b4 = ifelse(b1 > 35, (b1 - 35)^3, 0), b5 = ifelse(b1 > 65, (b1 - 65)^3, 0) ) p <- predict(lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3 + b4 + b5, data = d), newdata = newdat) ggplot(newdat, aes(x = b1, y = p)) + geom_point() + geom_vline(xintercept = c(4, 80), lty = 2) + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y))) ``` ::: ## Natural cubic splines {.small} *A natural cubic spline extrapolates linearly beyond the boundary knots* This adds 4 extra constraints and allows us to put **more** internal knots for the same degrees of freedom as a regular cubic spline ## Natural Cubic Splines {.small} :::{.panel-tabset} ### Plot ```{r} #| echo: false p <- predict(lm(y ~ splines::ns(b1, knots = c(35, 65)), data = d), newdata = newdat) ggplot(newdat, aes(x = b1, y = p)) + geom_point() + geom_vline(xintercept = c(4, 80), lty = 2) + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y))) ``` ### Code ```{r} #| eval: false p <- predict(lm(y ~ splines::ns(b1, knots = c(35, 65)), data = d), newdata = newdat) ggplot(newdat, aes(x = b1, y = p)) + geom_point() + geom_vline(xintercept = c(4, 80), lty = 2) + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y))) ``` ::: ## Natural Cubic Splines {.small} :::{.panel-tabset} ### Plot ```{r} #| echo: false da <- tibble( x = newdat$b1, ns = predict(lm(y ~ splines::ns(b1, knots = c(35, 65)), data = d), newdata = newdat), cubic = predict(lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3 + b4 + b5, data = d), newdata = newdat), linear = predict(lm(y ~ b1 + ifelse(b1>35, b1 - 35, 0) + ifelse(b1>65, b1 - 65, 0), data = d), newdata = newdat) ) |> pivot_longer(ns:linear) da |> filter(name != "linear") |> ggplot(aes(x = x, y = value, color = name)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + geom_vline(xintercept = c(4, 80), lty = 2) + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y)), color = "Spline") ``` ### Code ```{r} #| eval: false da <- tibble( x = newdat$b1, ns = predict(lm(y ~ splines::ns(b1, knots = c(35, 65)), data = d), newdata = newdat), cubic = predict(lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3 + b4 + b5, data = d), newdata = newdat), linear = predict(lm(y ~ b1 + ifelse(b1>35, b1 - 35, 0) + ifelse(b1>65, b1 - 65, 0), data = d), newdata = newdat) ) |> pivot_longer(ns:linear) da |> filter(name != "linear") |> ggplot(aes(x = x, y = value, color = name)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + geom_vline(xintercept = c(4, 80), lty = 2) + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y)), color = "Spline") ``` ::: ## Natural Splines {.small} ```{r} ggplot(da, aes(x = x, y = value, color = name)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + geom_vline(xintercept = c(4, 80), lty = 2) + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y)), color = "Spline") ``` ## Knot placement {.small} - One strategy is to decide $K$ (the number of knots) in advance and then place them at appropriate quantiles of the observed $X$ - A cubic spline with $K$ knots has $K+3$ parameters (or degrees of freedom!) - A natural spline with $K$ knots has $K-1$ degrees of freedom ## Knot placement {.small} Here is a comparison of a degree-14 polynomial and natural cubic spline (both have 15 degrees of freedom) ## Acknowledgements {.smaller} The content in the slides is from - Chapter 7 of [Introduction to Statistical Learning, 2nd Ed](https://hastie.su.domains/ISLR2/ISLRv2_corrected_June_2023.pdf.download.html) by James, Witten, Hastie, and Tibshirani - Initial versions of the slides are by Dr. Lucy D’Agostino McGowan

Polynomials! ## Polynomials {.smaller} $$y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_i + \beta_2x_i^2+\beta_3x_i^3 \dots + \beta_dx_i^d+\epsilon_i$$ . . . :::{.panel-tabset} ### Plot ```{r, echo = FALSE,out.width= "70%"} #| fig-height: 4.5 ggplot(co, aes(age, pop)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(formula = y ~ poly(x, 4), method = "lm") ``` ### Code ```{r, eval = F} ggplot(co, aes(age, pop)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(formula = y ~ poly(x, 4), method = "lm") ``` :::{.aside} This is data from the Columbia World Fertility Survey (1975-76) to examine household compositions ::: ::: ## How is it done? {.small} - New variables are created ( $X_1 = X$, $X_2 = X^2$, $X_3 = X^3$, etc) and treated as multiple linear regression - We are *not* interested in the individual coefficients, we are interested in how a *specific* $x$ value behaves - $\hat{f}(x_0) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1x_0 + \hat\beta_2x_0^2 + \hat\beta_3x_0^3 + \hat\beta_4x_0^4$ - *or more often a change between two values*, $a$ and $b$ - $\hat{f}(b) -\hat{f}(a) = \hat\beta_1b + \hat\beta_2b^2 + \hat\beta_3b^3 + \hat\beta_4b^4 - \hat\beta_1a - \hat\beta_2a^2 - \hat\beta_3a^3 -\hat\beta_4a^4$ - $\hat{f}(b) -\hat{f}(a) =\hat\beta_1(b-a) + \hat\beta_2(b^2-a^2)+\hat\beta_3(b^3-a^3)+\hat\beta_4(b^4-a^4)$ ## Polynomial Regression {.small} $$\hat{f}(b) -\hat{f}(a) =\hat\beta_1(b-a) + \hat\beta_2(b^2-a^2)+\hat\beta_3(b^3-a^3)+\hat\beta_4(b^4-a^4)$$ ::: question How do you pick $a$ and $b$? ::: - If given no other information, a sensible choice may be the 25th and 75th percentiles of $x$ ## Polynomial Regression :::{.panel-tabset} ### Plot ```{r, echo = FALSE} ggplot(co, aes(x = age, y = pop)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(formula = y ~ poly(x, 4), method = "lm") + geom_vline(xintercept = c(24.5, 73.5), lty = 2) ``` ### Code ```{r, eval = FALSE} ggplot(co, aes(x = age, y = pop)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(formula = y ~ poly(x, 4), method = "lm") + geom_vline(xintercept = c(24.5, 73.5), lty = 2) ``` ::: ## `Application Exercise` {.smaller} $$pop = \beta_0 + \beta_1age + \beta_2age^2 + \beta_3age^3 +\beta_4age^4+ \epsilon$$ . . . ::: question Using the information below, write out the equation to predicted change in population from a change in age from the 25th percentile (24.5) to a 75th percentile (73.5). ::: :::{.panel-tabset} ### Model Result ```{r, echo = FALSE} lm(pop ~ age + I(age^2) + I(age^3) + I(age^4), data = co) %>% tidy() %>% knitr::kable(digits = 4, format = "markdown") ``` ### Code ```{r, eval = FALSE} lm(pop ~ age + I(age^2) + I(age^3) + I(age^4), data = co) %>% tidy() ``` ::: ## Choosing $d$ {.small} $$y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_i + \beta_2x_i^2+\beta_3x_i^3 \dots + \beta_dx_i^d+\epsilon_i$$ ### Either: ::: nonincremental - Pre-specify $d$ (before looking `r emo::ji("eyes")` at your data!) - Use cross-validation to pick $d$ (take statistical learning!) ::: . . . ::: question Why before looking? ::: ## Polynomial Regression Polynomials have notoriously bad tail behavior (so they can be bad for extrapolation) . . . ::: question What does this mean? ::: ## Step functions {.smaller} Another way to create a transformation is to cut the variable into distinct regions $$C_1(X) = I(X < 35), C_2(X) = I(35\leq X<65), C_3(X) = I(X \geq 65)$$ . . . :::{.panel-tabset} ### Plot ```{r, echo = FALSE,out.width="60%"} #| fig-height: 4.5 mod <- lm(pop ~ I(age < 35) + I(age >=35 & age < 65) + I(age >= 65), data = co) p <- predict(mod) ggplot(co, aes(x = age, y = pop)) + geom_point() + geom_line(aes(x = age, y = p), color = "blue") ``` ### Code ```{r, eval = FALSE} mod <- lm(pop ~ I(age < 35) + I(age >=35 & age < 65) + I(age >= 65), data = co) p <- predict(mod) ggplot(co, aes(x = age, y = pop)) + geom_point() + geom_line(aes(x = age, y = p), color = "blue") ``` ::: ## Step functions {.small} - Create dummy variables for each group - Include each of these variables in multiple regression - The choice of cutpoints or **knots** can be problematic (and make a big difference!) ## Step functions {.small} $$C_1(X) = I(X < 35), C_2(X) = I(35\leq X<65), C_3(X) = I(X \geq 65)$$ :::{.panel-tabset} ### Plot ```{r, echo = FALSE} #| fig-height: 2.5 mod <- lm(pop ~ I(age < 35) + I(age >=35 & age < 65) + I(age >= 65), data = co) p <- predict(mod) ggplot(co, aes(x = age, y = pop)) + geom_point() + geom_line(aes(x = age, y = p), color = "blue") ``` ### Code ```{r, eval = FALSE} mod <- lm(pop ~ I(age < 35) + I(age >=35 & age < 65) + I(age >= 65), data = co) p <- predict(mod) ggplot(co, aes(x = age, y = pop)) + geom_point() + geom_line(aes(x = age, y = p), color = "blue") ``` ::: . . . ::: question What is the predicted value when $age = 25$? ::: ## Step functions {.small} $$C_1(X) = I(X < 15), C_2(X) = I(15\leq X<65), C_3(X) = I(X \geq 65)$$ :::{.panel-tabset} ### Plot ```{r, echo = FALSE} #| fig-height: 2.5 mod <- lm(pop ~ I(age < 15) + I(age >=15 & age < 65) + I(age >= 65), data = co) p <- predict(mod) ggplot(co, aes(x = age, y = pop)) + geom_point() + geom_line(aes(x = age, y = p), color = "blue") ``` ### Code ```{r, eval = FALSE} mod <- lm(pop ~ I(age < 15) + I(age >=15 & age < 65) + I(age >= 65), data = co) p <- predict(mod) ggplot(co, aes(x = age, y = pop)) + geom_point() + geom_line(aes(x = age, y = p), color = "blue") ``` ::: . . . ::: question What is the predicted value when $age = 25$? ::: ## Piecewise polynomials {.small} Instead of a single polynomial in $X$ over it's whole domain, we can use different polynomials in regions defined by knots $$y_i = \begin{cases}\beta_{01}+\beta_{11}x_i + \beta_{21}x^2_i+\beta_{31}x^3_i+\epsilon_i& \textrm{if } x_i < c\\ \beta_{02}+\beta_{12}x_i + \beta_{22}x_i^2 + \beta_{32}x_{i}^3+\epsilon_i&\textrm{if }x_i\geq c\end{cases}$$ ::: question What could go wrong here? ::: - It would be nice to have constraints (like continuity!) - Insert **splines!** ## Examples ![](img/splines.png) ## Linear Splines {.small} *A linear spline with knots at* $\xi_k$, $k = 1,\dots, K$ is a piecewise linear polynomial continuous at each knot $$y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1b_1(x_i)+\beta_2b_2(x_i)+\dots+\beta_{K+1}b_{K+1}(x_i)+\epsilon_i$$ - $b_k$ are **basis functions** - $\begin{align}b_1(x_i)&=x_i\\ b_{k+1}(x_i)&=(x_i-\xi_k)_+,k=1,\dots,K\end{align}$ - Here $()_+$ means the **positive part** - $(x_i-\xi_k)_+=\begin{cases}x_i-\xi_k & \textrm{if } x_i>\xi_k\\0&\textrm{otherwise}\end{cases}$ ## `Application Exercise` {.small} Let's create data set to fit a *linear spline* with 2 knots: 35 and 65. :::: columns ::: {.column width="20%"} | x | |-----| | 4 | | 15 | | 25 | | 37 | | 49 | | 66 | |70 | |80 | ::: ::: {.column width="80%"} ::: nonincremental 1. Using the data to the left create a new dataset with three variables: $b_1(x), b_2(x), b_3(x)$ 2. Write out the equation you would be fitting to estimate the effect on some outcome $y$ using this linear spline ::: ::: :::: ## Linear Spline :::: columns ::: {.column width="20%"} | x | |-----| | 4 | | 15 | | 25 | | 37 | | 49 | | 66 | |70 | |80 | ::: ::: {.column width="10%"} ### `r emo::ji("right_arrow")` ::: ::: {.column width="70%"} | $b_1(x)$| $b_2(x)$ | $b_3(x)$| |-----|--------------|---------| | 4 | 0 | 0 | 15 | 0 | 0 | 25 | 0 | 0 | 37 | 2 | 0 | 49 | 14 | 0 | 66 | 31 | 1 |70 | 35 | 5 |80 | 45 | 15 ::: :::: ## `Application Exercise` {.small} Below is a linear regression model fit to include the 3 bases you just created with 2 knots: 35 and 65. Use the information here to draw the relationship between $x$ and $y$. :::{.panel-tabset} ### Result ```{r} #| echo: false set.seed(1) d <- tibble( b1 = c(4, 15, 25, 37, 49, 66, 70, 80), b2 = ifelse(b1 < 35, 0, b1 - 35), b3 = ifelse(b1 < 65, 0, b1 - 65), y = 2 * b1 + -2 * b2 -3 * b3 + rnorm(8, sd = 0.25) ) lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3, data = d) |> tidy() |> knitr::kable(digits = 1) ``` ### Code ```{r} #| eval: false set.seed(1) d <- tibble( b1 = c(4, 15, 25, 37, 49, 66, 70, 80), b2 = ifelse(b1 < 35, 0, b1 - 35), b3 = ifelse(b1 < 65, 0, b1 - 65), y = 2 * b1 + -2 * b2 -3 * b3 + rnorm(8, sd = 0.25) ) lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3, data = d) |> tidy() |> knitr::kable(digits = 1) ``` ::: ## Linear Splines {.small} ::: {.column width="70%"} | $b_1(x)$| $b_2(x)$ | $b_3(x)$| $\hat{y}$ |-----|--------------|---------| | 4 | 0 | 0 | $2 \times 4 -2 \times 0 - 3\times 0 = 8$ | 15 | 0 | 0 | $2 \times 15 -2 \times 0 - 3\times 0 = 30$ | 25 | 0 | 0 | $2 \times 25 -2 \times 0 - 3\times 0 = 50$ | 37 | 2 | 0 | $2 \times 37 -2 \times 2 - 3\times 0 = 70$ | 49 | 14 | 0 | $2 \times 49 -2 \times 14 - 3\times 0 = 70$ | 66 | 31 | 1 | $2 \times 66 -2 \times 31 - 3\times 1 = 67$ |70 | 35 | 5 | $2 \times 70 -2 \times 35 - 3\times 5 = 55$ |80 | 45 | 15 | $2 \times 80 -2 \times 45 - 3\times 15 = 25$ ::: ## Linear Splines {.small} :::{.panel-tabset} ### Plot ```{r} #| echo: false p_ <- predict(lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3, data = d)) ggplot(d, aes(x = b1, y = p_)) + geom_point() + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y))) ``` ### Code ```{r} #| eval: false p_ <- predict(lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3, data = d)) ggplot(d, aes(x = b1, y = p_)) + geom_point() + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y))) ``` ::: ## Linear Splines {.small} :::{.panel-tabset} ### Plot ```{r} #| echo: false newdat <- tibble( b1 = 4:80, b2 = ifelse(b1 > 35, b1 - 35, 0), b3 = ifelse(b1 > 65, b1 - 65, 0) ) p <- predict(lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3, data = d), newdata = newdat) ggplot(newdat, aes(x = b1, y = p)) + geom_point() + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y))) ``` ### Code ```{r} #| eval: false newdat <- tibble( b1 = 4:80, b2 = ifelse(b1 > 35, b1 - 35, 0), b3 = ifelse(b1 > 65, b1 - 65, 0) ) p <- predict(lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3, data = d), newdata = newdat) ggplot(newdat, aes(x = b1, y = p)) + geom_point() + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y))) ``` ::: ## Cubic Splines {.small} *A cubic splines with knots at* $\xi_i, k = 1, \dots, K$ is a piecewise cubic polynomial with continuous derivatives up to order 2 at each knot. Again we can represent this model with truncated power functions $$y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1b_1(x_i)+\beta_2b_2(x_i)+\dots+\beta_{K+3}b_{K+3}(x_i) + \epsilon_i$$ $$\begin{align}b_1(x_i)&=x_i\\b_2(x_i)&=x_i^2\\b_3(x_i)&=x_i^3\\b_{k+3}(x_i)&=(x_i-\xi_k)^3_+, k = 1,\dots,K\end{align}$$ where $$(x_i-\xi_k)^{3}_+=\begin{cases}(x_i-\xi_k)^3&\textrm{if }x_i>\xi_k\\0&\textrm{otherwise}\end{cases}$$ ## `Application Exercise` {.small} Let's create data set to fit a *cubic spline* with 2 knots: 35 and 65. :::: columns ::: {.column width="20%"} | x | |-----| | 4 | | 15 | | 25 | | 37 | | 49 | | 66 | |70 | |80 | ::: ::: {.column width="80%"} ::: nonincremental 1. Using the data to the left create a new dataset with five variables: $b_1(x), b_2(x), b_3(x), b_4(x), b_5(x)$ 2. Write out the equation you would be fitting to estimate the effect on some outcome *y* using this cubic spline ::: ::: :::: ## Cubic Spline {.smaller} :::{.panel-tabset} ### Example :::: columns ::: {.column width="20%"} | x | |-----| | 4 | | 15 | | 25 | | 37 | | 49 | | 66 | |70 | |80 | ::: ::: {.column width="10%"} #### `r emo::ji("right_arrow")` ::: ::: {.column width="70%"} ```{r} #| echo: false d |> mutate(b2 = b1^2, b3 = b1^3, b4 = ifelse(b1 > 35, (b1 - 35)^3, 0), b5 = ifelse(b1 > 65, (b1 - 65)^3, 0) ) -> d d |> select(-y) |> knitr::kable() ``` ::: :::: ### Code ```{r} #| eval: false d |> mutate(b2 = b1^2, b3 = b1^3, b4 = ifelse(b1 > 35, (b1 - 35)^3, 0), b5 = ifelse(b1 > 65, (b1 - 65)^3, 0) ) -> d d |> select(-y) |> knitr::kable() ``` ::: ## Cubic Spline {.small} :::{.panel-tabset} ### Fit Result ```{r} #| echo: false lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3 + b4 + b5, data = d) |> tidy() |> knitr::kable(digits = 3) ``` ### Code ```{r} #| eval: false lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3 + b4 + b5, data = d) |> tidy() |> knitr::kable(digits = 3) ``` ::: ## Cubic Splines {.small} :::{.panel-tabset} ### Plot ```{r} #| echo: false p_ <- predict(lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3 + b4 + b5, data = d)) ggplot(d, aes(x = b1, y = p_)) + geom_point() + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y))) ``` ### Code ```{r} #| eval: false p_ <- predict(lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3 + b4 + b5, data = d)) ggplot(d, aes(x = b1, y = p_)) + geom_point() + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y))) ``` ::: ## Cubic Splines {.small} :::{.panel-tabset} ### Plot ```{r} #| echo: false newdat <- tibble( b1 = 4:80, b2 = b1^2, b3 = b1^3, b4 = ifelse(b1 > 35, (b1 - 35)^3, 0), b5 = ifelse(b1 > 65, (b1 - 65)^3, 0) ) p <- predict(lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3 + b4 + b5, data = d), newdata = newdat) ggplot(newdat, aes(x = b1, y = p)) + geom_point() + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y))) ``` ### Code ```{r} #| eval: false newdat <- tibble( b1 = 4:80, b2 = b1^2, b3 = b1^3, b4 = ifelse(b1 > 35, (b1 - 35)^3, 0), b5 = ifelse(b1 > 65, (b1 - 65)^3, 0) ) p <- predict(lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3 + b4 + b5, data = d), newdata = newdat) ggplot(newdat, aes(x = b1, y = p)) + geom_point() + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y))) ``` ::: ## Cubic Splines {.small} :::{.panel-tabset} ### Plot ```{r} #| echo: false newdat <- tibble( b1 = -100:100, b2 = b1^2, b3 = b1^3, b4 = ifelse(b1 > 35, (b1 - 35)^3, 0), b5 = ifelse(b1 > 65, (b1 - 65)^3, 0) ) p <- predict(lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3 + b4 + b5, data = d), newdata = newdat) ggplot(newdat, aes(x = b1, y = p)) + geom_point() + geom_vline(xintercept = c(4, 80), lty = 2) + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y))) ``` ### Code ```{r} #| eval: false newdat <- tibble( b1 = -100:100, b2 = b1^2, b3 = b1^3, b4 = ifelse(b1 > 35, (b1 - 35)^3, 0), b5 = ifelse(b1 > 65, (b1 - 65)^3, 0) ) p <- predict(lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3 + b4 + b5, data = d), newdata = newdat) ggplot(newdat, aes(x = b1, y = p)) + geom_point() + geom_vline(xintercept = c(4, 80), lty = 2) + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y))) ``` ::: ## Natural cubic splines {.small} *A natural cubic spline extrapolates linearly beyond the boundary knots* This adds 4 extra constraints and allows us to put **more** internal knots for the same degrees of freedom as a regular cubic spline ## Natural Cubic Splines {.small} :::{.panel-tabset} ### Plot ```{r} #| echo: false p <- predict(lm(y ~ splines::ns(b1, knots = c(35, 65)), data = d), newdata = newdat) ggplot(newdat, aes(x = b1, y = p)) + geom_point() + geom_vline(xintercept = c(4, 80), lty = 2) + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y))) ``` ### Code ```{r} #| eval: false p <- predict(lm(y ~ splines::ns(b1, knots = c(35, 65)), data = d), newdata = newdat) ggplot(newdat, aes(x = b1, y = p)) + geom_point() + geom_vline(xintercept = c(4, 80), lty = 2) + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y))) ``` ::: ## Natural Cubic Splines {.small} :::{.panel-tabset} ### Plot ```{r} #| echo: false da <- tibble( x = newdat$b1, ns = predict(lm(y ~ splines::ns(b1, knots = c(35, 65)), data = d), newdata = newdat), cubic = predict(lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3 + b4 + b5, data = d), newdata = newdat), linear = predict(lm(y ~ b1 + ifelse(b1>35, b1 - 35, 0) + ifelse(b1>65, b1 - 65, 0), data = d), newdata = newdat) ) |> pivot_longer(ns:linear) da |> filter(name != "linear") |> ggplot(aes(x = x, y = value, color = name)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + geom_vline(xintercept = c(4, 80), lty = 2) + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y)), color = "Spline") ``` ### Code ```{r} #| eval: false da <- tibble( x = newdat$b1, ns = predict(lm(y ~ splines::ns(b1, knots = c(35, 65)), data = d), newdata = newdat), cubic = predict(lm(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3 + b4 + b5, data = d), newdata = newdat), linear = predict(lm(y ~ b1 + ifelse(b1>35, b1 - 35, 0) + ifelse(b1>65, b1 - 65, 0), data = d), newdata = newdat) ) |> pivot_longer(ns:linear) da |> filter(name != "linear") |> ggplot(aes(x = x, y = value, color = name)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + geom_vline(xintercept = c(4, 80), lty = 2) + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y)), color = "Spline") ``` ::: ## Natural Splines {.small} ```{r} ggplot(da, aes(x = x, y = value, color = name)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + geom_vline(xintercept = c(4, 80), lty = 2) + labs(x = "X", y = expression(hat(y)), color = "Spline") ``` ## Knot placement {.small} - One strategy is to decide $K$ (the number of knots) in advance and then place them at appropriate quantiles of the observed $X$ - A cubic spline with $K$ knots has $K+3$ parameters (or degrees of freedom!) - A natural spline with $K$ knots has $K-1$ degrees of freedom ## Knot placement {.small} Here is a comparison of a degree-14 polynomial and natural cubic spline (both have 15 degrees of freedom) ## Acknowledgements {.smaller} The content in the slides is from - Chapter 7 of [Introduction to Statistical Learning, 2nd Ed](https://hastie.su.domains/ISLR2/ISLRv2_corrected_June_2023.pdf.download.html) by James, Witten, Hastie, and Tibshirani - Initial versions of the slides are by Dr. Lucy D’Agostino McGowan
